title: Relationships and joins
summary: How tables connect (one-to-many, many-to-many) and how a JOIN puts the pieces back together for a screen.
youWillLearn: The three shapes of relationship, and where the link lives for each
How a JOIN matches rows, and when you need a left join
How to spot the N+1 query trap in code Claude Code writes

glossary.relationship: How rows in two tables belong together, like a note belonging to a user.
glossary.one-to-one: Each row on one side matches at most one row on the other, like a user and their profile.
glossary.one-to-many: One row on one side matches many on the other, like one user with many notes, each note with one owner.
glossary.many-to-many: Rows on both sides can match many on the other, like notes and tags.
glossary.foreign key: A column that stores the primary key of a row in another table, checked by the database.
glossary.join table: A table whose rows each link one row from one table to one row from another, used for many-to-many.
glossary.JOIN: The part of a SQL query that combines rows from two tables wherever a key matches.
glossary.inner join: A join that keeps only rows that found a match on both sides. It is what a plain join does.
glossary.left join: A join that keeps every row from the first table, filling the other side with null when there is no match.
glossary.index: A sorted lookup Postgres keeps for a column, like the index at the back of a book, so it can find matching rows without reading the whole table.
glossary.N+1 query: Fetching a list with one query, then running one more query per item. Slow, and it grows with the list.

steps.title: Three tables, one screen
body: Maya's note list shows, for each note, the title, the author's name and some tag chips. In the database those facts live in three tables: notes, users and tags.
Each table holds its own facts once, as lesson 1 set up. The screen needs them side by side. Something has to put the pieces back together, quickly and correctly.

scene.caption: One screen needs facts from three separate tables.

steps.title: Three shapes of relationship
body: Tables connect in three shapes. One-to-one: a user has one profile. One-to-many: a user has many notes, each note has one owner. Many-to-many: a note has many tags, and a tag sits on many notes.
Name the shape of each relationship first. It tells you where the link must live.

callout.text: An author and their books is one-to-many: each book has one author. Students and classes is many-to-many: the school keeps a class register to record who is in what.

scene.caption: Users to notes is one-to-many. Notes to tags is many-to-many.

steps.title: One-to-many: the key sits on the many side
body: Each note has exactly one owner, so the note can carry the owner's id. That is the user_id foreign key from lesson 1.

Never the other way round. A user row cannot keep a list of note ids in one column: the list would grow forever, and the database could not check each id. One-to-one works the same way, plus a unique rule on the key.

scene.caption: Each note carries one user_id. A user carries nothing about its notes.

steps.title: Many-to-many needs a table in the middle
body: A note has many tags and a tag has many notes, so neither side can hold a single id. The fix is a third table, a join table: note_tags. Each row says "this note has this tag".
It holds two foreign keys. Together they form its primary key, so the same tag cannot land on a note twice.

code.caption: on delete cascade: when a note is deleted, its tag links go with it.

scene.caption: note_tags sits between notes and tags. Each row is one note-tag pair.

steps.title: JOIN glues rows back together
body: A JOIN lines up rows from two tables wherever a key matches. For each note, Postgres finds the user whose id equals the note's user_id, and returns one combined row.
You describe the match. The database decides the fastest way to find it.

code.code:
select notes.title, users.name as author
from notes
join users on users.id = notes.user_id
where notes.user_id = 7;
code.caption: Each result row: a note's title next to its author's name.

scene.caption: Rows from notes and users meet where user_id matches id.

steps.title: Inner vs left: who gets dropped
body: A plain join is an inner join: rows with no match vanish. Join notes to tags that way and every untagged note disappears from Maya's list.
A left join keeps every row from the first table and fills the missing side with null. Rule of thumb: if the other side is optional, use left join.

code.code:
select notes.title, tags.name as tag
from notes
left join note_tags on note_tags.note_id = notes.id
left join tags on tags.id = note_tags.tag_id;
code.caption: An untagged note still appears once, with tag = null.

scene.caption: Joined through note_tags. A left join keeps notes that have no tags.

steps.title: Supabase follows the keys for you
body: In Notely's Next.js code you rarely write the join by hand. The Supabase client reads your foreign keys and nests related rows in the result.

This one call returns each note with its author and its tags, through note_tags, as nested JSON. It only works because the foreign keys are declared. Plain id columns without references give Supabase nothing to follow.

code.code:
const { data, error } = await supabase
  .from('notes')
  .select('id, title, users ( name ), tags ( name )')
  .order('created_at', { ascending: false });
code.caption: One request, one query. Result: [{ title, users: { name }, tags: [{ name }] }]

scene.caption: One call fetches notes, authors and tags together for the screen.

steps.title: The N+1 query trap
body: A classic slow page: fetch 50 notes, then loop and fetch each note's author one by one. That is 1 query plus 50 more, the N+1 query problem.
Each round trip to the database costs a few milliseconds. Fine on your laptop with five notes. Painful in production with hundreds. One joined query does the same work in one trip.

callout.text: Look for await inside a loop, or a .map() that calls the database. Ask Claude Code: "Can this be one query with a join or a nested select?" Also check that foreign key columns like notes.user_id have an index. Postgres does not add one for you.

scene.caption: One query for the list, then one more per note. The page waits on 51 trips.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Name the shape first. One-to-many: a foreign key on the many side. Many-to-many: a join table holding two foreign keys. A JOIN rebuilds the picture by matching keys; use a left join when the other side is optional.
Fetch related data in one query, never one query per row.

scene.caption: Keys in the right places, and one query that follows them.

quiz.question: Notely adds folders. Each note sits in exactly one folder, and a folder holds many notes. Where does the link go?

options.why: A list in one column grows forever and the database cannot check each id inside it. The key belongs on the many side.
One-to-many: each note has one folder, so the note carries the folder's id, like user_id.
That would allow a note in many folders, which you do not want, and adds a table for nothing. Join tables are for many-to-many.

quiz.question: You join notes to tags with a plain join. Maya says her untagged notes vanished from the list. What is the fix?

options.text: Use left join for the tag tables.
options.why: A left join keeps every note and fills the tag with null when there is none.

options.text: Give every note a fake "untagged" tag.
options.why: It hides the symptom by adding junk data that every other feature then has to filter out.
That removes rows without tags, which is the opposite of what Maya wants.

quiz.question: Claude Code wrote a page that loads 100 notes, then runs for (const note of notes) { await supabase.from('users')… }. What do you ask for?

options.text: Nothing. await keeps the results in the right order.
options.why: Order is not the problem. 101 round trips to the database is, and it grows with every note.

options.text: Run the loop in the browser instead of on the server.
options.why: It is the same 101 queries, now each one crossing the user's slower network. Moving the loop does not remove it.

options.text: One query that fetches notes with their authors, using a join or a nested select.
options.why: This is an N+1 query. One joined query returns the same data in one trip.

takeaways: One-to-many: put the foreign key on the many side (notes.user_id).
Many-to-many: add a join table with two foreign keys that together form its primary key.
A plain join drops rows without a match. Use left join when the other side is optional.
An await inside a loop that queries the database is an N+1 bug. Ask for one query.
